description: We are CS students from FAST-NUCES Karachi, passionate about space, education, and building projects people enjoy. Our team is already formed and taking on “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer.” We’re building a game-style web app that teaches kids how astronauts train: space quizzes, a mission simulator (fuel, oxygen, food), a launch checklist game, and badges. We’ll use real NASA data and APIs, and focus on delivering a polished, working demo.
summary:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a browser-based survival game that teaches how to keep a Moon or Mars base alive. Players choose Mars (Jezero Crater) or the Moon (Artemis Base) and Cadet Mode (ages 7–12) or Flight Director Mode (ages 13+), fly a 3D spaceship landing for bonus supplies, then run the base in a 2D view. To win, they survive 30 Sols and earn 1,000 science points.

Oxygen, power, food, water, heat and radiation are all linked, so every choice causes a chain reaction. Turning off heaters saves power, but cold batteries lose capacity. Players reorder a 5-level power priority list, adjust shielding, and manage crops and the CO2 scrubber while facing four emergencies: solar radiation storms, power shortages, late supply ships, and scrubber failure. Storm alerts use real NASA DONKI solar flare data, with saved 2003 storm data as an offline backup.

When a mission fails, a NASA-style Mishap Board shows a cause-and-effect chart that points to the first mistake, and Time Rewind lets players retry from an earlier Sol.

Technically, the simulation core is written in C++ (built for WebAssembly) and updates the base hour by hour. A matching TypeScript engine runs it in the browser today. The interface uses React, Vite, Three.js, and React Flow.
details:
What it does and how it works

Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a browser game where the player runs a Moon or Mars base and must keep the crew alive. The player picks Mars (Jezero Crater) or the Moon (Artemis Base), then picks Cadet Mode (ages 7–12, simple words and colour-coded safety cues) or Flight Director Mode (ages 13+, full telemetry in kelvin, kPa, ppm, mSv and watts). Each mission starts with a 3D spaceship landing. A good landing earns bonus food, water and science points. The player then runs the base in a 2D view, clicking through rooms and systems. To win, the crew must survive 30 Sols (space days) and earn 1,000 science points.

The base is a set of linked systems: oxygen, CO2, power, food, water, heat, radiation and crew health. Every choice causes a chain reaction. If the player turns off heaters to save power, the cabin cools, cold batteries lose capacity, and power gets even tighter. More radiation shielding protects the crew but blocks light for the crops. Players manage a reorderable 5-level power priority list, a CO2 scrubber, a Sabatier water-recovery reactor, hydroponic crops, solar panel cleaning, and a storm shelter. Three AI crew advisors give tips, and when CO2 is high their messages become garbled, like real cognitive impairment.

Four emergencies test the player: solar radiation storms, power shortages (dust storm or lunar night), late supply ships, and scrubber failure. Storm alerts use real NASA DONKI solar flare data. If the live service is unavailable, the game falls back to saved data from the 2003 Halloween solar storms.

When a mission fails, the game opens a NASA-style Mishap Board instead of a plain “Game Over”. It shows a cause-and-effect graph of logged events that points to the first mistake. The player can then use Time Rewind to go back to an earlier Sol and try a better decision.

Benefits and intended impact

Players learn systems thinking by trying things: make a choice, see what happens, find out why, and do better next time. The game shows why space habitats are engineering trade-offs rather than single problems, and it is easy to run in a classroom because it needs no download and no server.

Tools, languages and software

  • C++ for the core simulation (physics solver, event engine, mishap recorder). It steps the base forward one hour at a time. It is built and tested with CMake and CTest, and can be compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten.
  • TypeScript for a matching copy of the simulation engine. It currently runs in the browser; the WebAssembly connection is built but not fully wired up yet.
  • React, TypeScript and Vite for the interface.
  • Three.js and React Three Fiber for the 3D landing and base view.
  • React Flow for the cause-and-effect graph.
  • NASA DONKI for solar flare data.

No special hardware is needed. It runs in a normal web browser.

How it is creative

Instead of a “Game Over” screen, failure becomes a learning tool through the Mishap Board and Time Rewind. One simulation serves two audiences, kids and teens in Cadet Mode and older players in Flight Director Mode. Real NASA data drives the emergencies. Subtle effects such as frost, alarms, flickering lights and garbled advisors let players feel the state of the base, not just read numbers.

What our team considered

  • Reliability: the game runs fully in the browser, and every part has a fallback (the TypeScript engine, the saved NASA data), so it still works offline.
  • Accessibility: one shared simulation with two levels of presentation.
  • Explainability: every important event is logged with its cause, so failures can be explained.
  • Scope: we built the core loop first and added features after that, because working beats complete.

Some balance values are first-pass and still need tuning, and Time Rewind covers only the last 32 Sols.
